title: The real reason legal tech falls short
summary: How can your firm turn AI investments into measurable results? Explore five proven practices, informed by the firsthand experience of Intapp's Legal Strategic Advisory team.
body_markdown:
Most law firms don’t have a technology problem. They have an outcomes problem.


During my 30+ years in law firm leadership, I signed several technology contracts. I also dealt with what came after: the growth platform that became an expensive contact list, the rollout that stalled before go-live, and the tool that partners never opened.


None of those disappointments were really about software. They were about the failure to intentionally link technology features to concrete business outcomes — and to meet users where they work to improve adoption.


With AI investment accelerating, that gap is getting more expensive. Five practices separate the firms that see results from those that don’t. These aren’t theories; they’re lessons learned firsthand by Intapp’s Legal Strategic Advisory team, whose members have led the same functions our clients manage today.


### 1. Start with the outcome, not the feature list


Technology vendors often focus on features, not long-term business outcomes. Start by defining success in business terms — faster intake, higher realization, stronger relationships with key clients — then identify the capabilities needed to support it.


### 2. Treat the proposal as a roadmap


A technology purchase starts a multiyear change. Ask how the work will be phased, who owns each stage, and how progress will be measured. If the plan ends at go-live, it isn’t a plan.


### 3. Fund change management like the software


Adoption is where value is won or lost. Name an executive sponsor with real accountability, involve practice leaders early, and design training around how people actually work.


### 4. Build governance into AI from day one


The most valuable AI supports the business of the firm: intake, conflicts, pricing, realization, and growth. Those workflows carry client obligations, so governance can’t come later. Decide early on how tools are evaluated, what data they can reach, and how outputs are reviewed.


### 5. Design for the future state


Agentic AI changes what work can look like, not just how fast it gets done. Layer a new tool onto today’s process and you automate yesterday’s way of working. Decide first what the optimized state looks like — which work agents handle, where people add judgment, and which steps in the process disappear — then design the right combination of people, processes, and technology to achieve it. Make sure to involve your key stakeholders from the start. Partners, practice leaders, and business services teams will work differently when the tool goes live, so they should help shape what that looks like.
